title: A history of superconductivity: milestones and evidence
summary: Eighteen milestones from mercury to recent research, with original-source links, corrected chronology and the conditions behind reported temperatures.

review.scope: Eighteen stable historical milestones with corrected dates and temperature criteria. Prior original-source checks reused; selected Ginzburg and Josephson author retrospectives and the earlier LaOFeP report added.
limitations: Complete scientific acceptance remains open.
Original 1911, 1950 and 1962 full-text coverage is incomplete; later firsthand accounts are explicitly identified.
Several discovery papers remain abstract-only; original datasets, supplementary material and replication are not fully audited.
Narrative temperatures are not duplicate material records or a standardized record-ranking dataset.

claims.statement: The history of superconductivity includes discoveries, theories, material families and changing standards of evidence. These eighteen milestones preserve the approved topic identities while correcting dates and oversimplified temperature labels. A later author's recollection, an original discovery report and a modern reanalysis answer different historical questions. The cited review scope tells the reader which was checked.

claims.statement: There is no single mathematical curve that makes all reported transition temperatures directly comparable. A resistance onset, a midpoint, a noise-floor zero and a magnetic response can occur at different temperatures, even in one specimen. Pressure, composition, sample history and measurement field must remain attached to any point. The linked material articles preserve detailed records; this history does not create duplicate experimental Tc entries from narrative summaries.

claims.statement: Onnes's 1911 mercury work opened the study of superconductivity. His 1913 Nobel lecture provides a firsthand account of the abrupt resistance decrease near 4.2 K and the limits of the electrical measurement. Resistance too small to resolve is an experimental statement; mathematical exactness is not read directly from an instrument. The lecture also discusses a current threshold above which a voltage appeared, anticipating the need to specify measuring current.

The original 1911 communication itself remains outside the directly reviewed material; the author lecture is identified as the historical source used here.

claims.statement: Meissner and Ochsenfeld's 1933 work added magnetic behavior to the definition of the superconducting state. The selected original reproduction describes field redistribution around tin and lead as the samples became superconducting. This changed the question from whether a conductor can sustain current without detectable resistance to which magnetic state it reaches. An ideal conductor's history-dependent trapped field does not by itself supply the same equilibrium magnetic condition.

claims.statement: Geometry remains essential to reading the experiment. The original report also discusses retained field in a lead-tube cavity; a cavity is not the same region as the superconducting material. A simplified statement that every field everywhere becomes zero would erase this distinction. The historical paper's apparatus, uncertainty and complete translation have not been independently reconstructed here. The milestone records the new magnetic evidence while retaining the limits of the selected primary reproduction.

claims.statement: The London brothers' 1935 paper supplied an electromagnetic description of superconductors that accommodates magnetic screening. The selected original pages distinguish the consequence of perfect conductivity from an additional condition selecting the superconducting magnetic state. An integration constant associated with the initial field is therefore not a trivial detail: dropping it without stating the physical postulate would conceal what the theory adds.

claims.statement: The London description links current and electromagnetic fields under its stated local assumptions. It does not determine a material's microscopic pairing interaction or explain every spatially nonuniform state. Modern equations often use SI units and different notation from the original scan; a historical formula should not be copied into a modern calculation without checking those conventions. This milestone concerns a phenomenological advance in electrodynamics, not an experimental discovery of a new transition-temperature record.

claims.statement: Ginzburg and Landau introduced a complex order parameter and a free-energy description of superconductivity in 1950. Ginzburg's later firsthand lecture explains the motivation to extend the London treatment, including spatial variation and interfaces. The resulting framework connects electromagnetic response to the amplitude and phase of an order parameter and provides a basis for studying boundaries and competing configurations near a transition.

claims.statement: The history is not identical to today's textbook presentation. Ginzburg recounts that the effective charge was not correctly settled at twice the electron charge in the original work; the later microscopic interpretation clarified that point. Their early analysis also focused on what are now called type-I superconductors. Avoid projecting every subsequent vortex result or the complete BCS interpretation back into 1950. The checked source is the 2004 retrospective, with its original-paper citation, rather than a full direct audit of the 1950 article.

claims.statement: Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer's 1957 theory constructed a coherent paired many-electron state and related its excitation spectrum to superconducting observables. It moved beyond identifying macroscopic signatures by providing a microscopic explanation within a specified interaction model. The energy gap and thermodynamic behavior arise together in that framework, rather than being independent empirical labels attached to a zero-resistance state.

claims.statement: The achievement should not be turned into a claim that one elementary approximation describes every later material. The familiar isotropic weak-coupling results assume a particular pairing structure and energy-scale hierarchy. Strong coupling, multiple bands, unconventional symmetry and substantial fluctuations require further treatment. A historical timeline should distinguish the theory's established role from a material-specific mechanism assignment. Agreement with one BCS-like ratio is a consistency check, not proof that a newly observed superconductor has the same microscopic interaction.

claims.statement: Josephson's 1962 paper predicted new tunnelling effects between superconductors. His 1973 lecture distinguishes the theoretical prediction from the later experiments that convincingly attributed observed supercurrents to tunnelling. Earlier zero-voltage currents could instead have involved metallic shorts, and unsuccessful measurements were part of the development. Phase-dependent response, magnetic interference and microwave-induced voltage steps provided more specific tests than a zero-voltage branch alone.

claims.statement: The same approved milestone includes Jaccarino and Peter's 1962 proposal of ultra-high-field superconductivity through compensation of an external field by an internal exchange effect. This is a separate idea, not part of Josephson tunnelling. Its original bibliographic identity is checked here; the full original derivation is not. Later field-induced experiments and their limits are discussed in the linked exchange-compensation article. Keeping the two contributions distinct prevents a shared calendar year from becoming a misleading shared mechanism.

claims.statement: Processing is central to the historical interpretation: the source describes high-pressure sputtering, which is a deposition condition, not evidence that the superconducting transition was measured under high external pressure. Film composition, phase formation and preparation affect the result. Neither the reported temperature nor the A15 label defines a universal transition for all Nb–Ge samples or a strict ceiling for the entire structural family. Full methods and the exact operational transition criterion remain unreviewed at this abstract-level scope.

claims.statement: The 1979 CeCu2Si2 report established a superconducting state in a system with strong Pauli paramagnetism and an unusually large electronic response. Its original abstract gives a transition scale around 0.5 K. The historical importance lies in opening a strongly correlated setting for superconductivity, not in raising the maximum known transition temperature. Different measures of progress therefore belong in a scientific timeline.

claims.statement: This original observation should be separated from later debates over gap structure, magnetic coexistence and sample classification. Modern CeCu2Si2 experiments distinguish crystals and transitions that cannot be reduced to a universal 0.5 K constant. The presence of a heavy-electron normal state also does not uniquely identify a pairing interaction from the discovery abstract alone. The original full measurements have not been reconstructed in this review; the linked heavy-fermion article follows the subsequent evidence and its competing interpretations.

The publisher's original abstract describes multiphase polycrystals and a current-dependent, percolative resistive onset in the 30 K range. That is the evidence actually checked here. A precise bulk magnetic transition at 35 K should not be manufactured from the short planning label.

claims.statement: The milestone initiated a new materials direction, but the discovery report's sample and uncertainty deserve to remain visible. A connected superconducting path can strongly affect resistance without establishing that the whole sample occupies one superconducting phase. The original abstract and publication record were checked; the complete figures, apparatus and raw measurements remain outside this review scope. Historical significance does not remove the need to distinguish an initial report from later confirmation.

claims.statement: This was not the first superconducting iron-containing compound or even the first reported layered iron pnictide: the same research group's LaOFeP paper appeared in 2006. Iron-based materials subsequently require separate structural, magnetic and pairing analyses; the presence of iron does not fix a universal gap symmetry.
